questions.q: How does this lesson define what "system architecture" covers, as distinct from data or integration architecture specifically?
options: It is identical to data architecture, just a different name for the same thing
It's about how an org's data is modeled internally
It's the architecture of the overall landscape itself: how many orgs a business runs and how they relate to each other and the outside world
It only covers API design between two systems
questions.explain: System architecture sits above data and integration architecture — it asks how many Salesforce orgs a business should run and how they relate, before you've even designed what's inside any one of them.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of a single-org strategy, per this lesson?
options: It eliminates the need for any security configuration
It gives a unified data model and reporting layer across the whole business, without integration effort
It guarantees the org will never hit a platform limit
It is always cheaper in license cost than multi-org regardless of company size
questions.explain: A single org lets the business get a unified view — one data model, one set of users, one reporting layer that spans the whole company — without needing integration work to stitch data together across orgs.

questions.q: What is the real cost this lesson names for a multi-org strategy?
options: Multi-org strategies have no real costs at all
Every cross-org reporting need, shared process, or single customer view now requires integration work a single org would have gotten for free
Multi-org always violates Salesforce's terms of service
Multi-org eliminates the need for any licensing cost analysis
questions.explain: Splitting into multiple orgs genuinely helps with isolation and process fit, but it means losing the free unified view a single org provides — any cross-org need now requires real integration effort.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is a reasonable default approach to the single-org vs. multi-org decision, absent a hard separation need?
options: Always default to multi-org, since isolation is always safer
Always default to single-org and never reconsider it regardless of circumstances
Start with one org and only split when a specific, named reason justifies the added integration and governance cost
Flip a coin, since both options are equally valid in every situation
questions.explain: This lesson frames under-splitting (a slightly inconvenient single org) as usually cheaper than over-splitting (permanent integration overhead for an unneeded separation) — so starting with one org and splitting only for a specific, named reason is the reasonable default.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say licensing and org limits matter to a system architecture decision, not just to a budget conversation?
options: Because they are irrelevant to architecture and only matter to finance

Because a multi-org decision made purely on process-fit grounds, without checking license cost and per-org limits, is an incomplete analysis — the same kind of unverified assumption Lesson 7 warned about
Because Salesforce charges the same price regardless of how many orgs a company runs
Because org limits only apply to single-org strategies, never multi-org
questions.explain: Each org carries its own license costs, API limits, and administrative overhead. Ignoring that in a system architecture decision is an undocumented assumption at landscape scale, the same failure mode Lesson 7 covered for a single design.
